item.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis, nuanced discussion, and clear reporting on a significant educational issue.

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. The inspection that led to the downgrading of her primary school to “inadequate” was judged to have contributed to her death. In its 2024 manifesto, Labour promised to replace one-word labels with more nuanced overviews of schools’ performance.

But 12 months after the introduction of a report card to replace the old grades, Ofsted’s critics remain frustrated. The National Association of Head Teachers tried to challenge the revised framework in the high court. Two-thirds of teachers who responded to a survey said that the new inspections were as bad or worse than the old ones. In October the education secretary, Lucy Powell, said that further reforms were on the way. (After devolution in 1999, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland rejected England’s model of school competition, academies and league tables.)

If, as expected, the framework is adjusted to take more account of a school’s context, and to ease workload pressures, that will be a good result. Analysis shows that schools in England with more deprived intakes are much less likely than schools with low deprivation to meet expected standards. This raises questions about whether inspections fairly account for the challenges facing schools in poorer areas. As well as being wrong in principle, a framework skewed against demanding socioeconomic conditions has practical effects, lowering morale in schools that are judged to be underachieving, and potentially making it harder for them to recruit staff.

The Department for Education and Ofsted must take responsibility for such missteps, and for an inspection regime that many now find more onerous. Advocates of more radical reforms, whose goal is a less adversarial alternative to Ofsted, should be listened to as part of this process. Peer review between schools can be a constructive route to improvement. Local authorities already monitor standards in the schools they oversee, as do academy trusts – although their highly uneven results offer some of the best evidence of the need for an independent inspectorate with a focus on governance as well as other aspects. Resource pressures must also be considered; the current level of funding does not enable the kind of exchange between inspectors and schools that some would like.

It is shocking and tragic that Ofsted needed a coroner’s warning to seemingly recognise its duty to treat school staff with courtesy and respect. The new framework, evidence suggests, remains flawed. Ms Powell must ensure that inspections help schools improve, rather than merely find fault.

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-22 17:25 UTC | Difficulty: 62/100

Departing Providence Superintendent to Receive Nearly $200,000

The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez.

The Providence School Board approved a nearly $200,000 separation package for outgoing Providence Public School District Superintendent Javier Montañez at its Wednesday night meeting.

Montañez’s resignation — first announced on Oct. 30 and formally submitted in a Nov. 4 letter — took effect at the end of the day Wednesday. The separation comes about seven months before his contract was set to expire.

The separation agreement was approved in a unanimous 10-0 vote Wednesday night and provides the departing superintendent $152,706.92 in biweekly payments. The payments will begin on Friday and run through July 2, 2027.

Montañez will receive an additional $46,968.35 for a little over 54 days of unused vacation time. The unused holiday pay will be disbursed in five installments through mid-January, with the first installment also arriving on Friday.

Montañez will also retain his health insurance through June 30, 2027, and he will be responsible for his share of premiums.

The end of Montañez’s superintendency concludes his 30-year career in the Providence school system that began in 1996 when he was a bilingual second-grade teacher at what is now Spaziano Elementary School. Montañez eventually became the school’s assistant principal and then principal, before heading to Leviton Dual Language School to serve as principal for a decade.

He became superintendent in 2021, roughly two years into the state takeover of Providence’s public school system. The takeover ended on July 1, after nearly seven years.

In farewell remarks at the beginning of Wednesday’s meeting, Montañez urged board members to use their combined power to better the district and students alike.

“In order to hit greatness, you have to hit some bumps in the road,” Montañez said. “But you know what’s the difference between sitting there and becoming great is learning from those bumps.

“You know you can do great things,” he continued. “You have power. Learn how to use that power to benefit you and benefit our kids.”

Montañez spent his own school days in Providence’s classrooms. As a teenager he experienced homelessness and struggled with illiteracy and dyslexia before ultimately dropping out of Hope High School. He went on to obtain his GED and eventually a doctorate in educational leadership from Johnson & Wales University.

“I was one of those students that you said, ‘Oh, pobrecito Javier, he can’t do it,’” Montañez said. “Don’t do that. Challenge them, because they will end up surprising you.”

The separation agreement notes that Montañez and the board are in harmony on the idea that the district needs a new leader during this time of transition.

“The Board and Dr. Montanez now mutually agree that it is in the best interests of the District that the Board have an opportunity to hire a Superintendent of its own choosing to lead the District post state-takeover,” the agreement reads.

The separation agreement stipulates that Montañez will stay available to the district in a consulting capacity, specifically to aid incoming interim Superintendent Lendozia Edwards as she adjusts to her new job, which begins Thursday. Montañez’s consulting services will be available through June 30, and the agreement does not require him to report to district offices or work a certain number of hours.

Edwards was promoted from her current role as the district’s chief of schools to the interim superintendent position during a Saturday, Nov. 14 meeting of the school board, with the board formally approving her appointment at Wednesday’s meeting.

Edwards will serve as the district’s interim leader through June 30, 2028. Her salary is still being negotiated by the School Board. School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said at the meeting that he expects a contract will tentatively be ready by the board’s December meeting.

To mark the change in leadership, Montañez ceremonially gifted Edwards with a big key Wednesday night.

“I would like to give you the keys to the kingdom,” Montañez said. “And it’s heavy. I usually say the crown is heavy, but that key is heavy.”

Montañez’s contract with Rhode Island Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green was most recently renewed on July 1, 2024, and was set to expire on June 30, 2027. That contract stipulated the terms of his departure from the district, and allowed for the disbursement of Montañez’s remaining salary and benefits if he was terminated without cause, as well as compensation for up to 60 days of vacation time

Under the agreement, Montañez cannot receive compensation from the Rhode Island Department of Education through June 30, 2027.

The agreement also releases the board from an assortment of potential legal claims by Montañez, which could include alleged violations of state and federal laws governing employment, discrimination, civil rights and open meetings.

Excluded from this release is a workers’ compensation case filed in September. It is subject to a separate settlement.

As is common in such agreements, a non-disparagement clause prohibits Montañez and board members from making “knowingly false” statements, or statements “made with reckless disregard for the truth,” that could be “reasonably calculated to harm the individual’s reputation.”

This provision outlasts the end of Montañez’s payments as well as current board members’ terms in office.

“This provision applies from the beginning of the Parties’ relationship into the future, and the Parties agree that they shall never abandon this covenant,” the agreement reads.

But Montañez and the School Board had only good things to say about one another at Wednesday night’s meeting.…
